common_name: Magnifica Coral Honeysuckle (Compact Orange-Red Trumpet Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring or fall at the base of a trellis, mailbox post, or open fence in average, well-drained soil; Magnifica blooms most heavily in full sun but tolerates part shade.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, siting it at the base of a trellis, open fence, or mailbox post since it twines lightly and needs something narrow to grasp. Magnifica is a more compact coral honeysuckle selection, typically staying in the 4-7 foot range rather than sprawling 10-20 feet like the straight species, which makes it a better fit for smaller trellises and foundation plantings. Its tubular flowers open a vivid, saturated orange that reads brighter and more uniform than the reddish-orange-to-coral tones typical of unselected coral honeysuckle, and it blooms from spring through summer on both old and new wood, so light shaping can be done at almost any time without sacrificing the next flush. Small red berries follow the flowers and are readily taken by songbirds; like other native selections it is well-behaved and, unlike Japanese honeysuckle, will not escape into natural areas.

common_name: Superba Coral Honeysuckle (Bright Red Trumpet Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring near a trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained soil; stems twine and will climb 8-12 feet, so provide vertical support from the start.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light part shade at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor; Superba was selected for flowers that open a bright, clear red rather than the more orange-tinged red-to-coral of unselected coral honeysuckle, giving a bolder color contrast against its blue-green foliage. Whorled clusters of tubular red flowers open in spring with continued sporadic bloom into summer, drawing ruby-throated hummingbirds consistently through the season, and are followed by small red berries that songbirds strip quickly. It twines rather than clings, so give it wire, lattice, or twiggy branches to grasp, and prune right after the main spring flush to control size and maintain a full habit. Like other coral honeysuckle selections it is a well-behaved native that will not spread invasively the way Japanese honeysuckle does.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
